clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant hypocalcaemia is essentially the biochemical mirror image of familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia: the same calcium-sensing receptor gene is involved, but with a gain-of-function rather than a loss-of-function change.

The hallmark is hypocalcaemia accompanied by an inappropriately low or 'normal' parathyroid hormone level, in contrast to most other causes of hypocalcaemia where parathyroid hormone rises appropriately.
Relative hypercalciuria is the distinguishing renal feature: patients continue to waste calcium in the urine despite being hypocalcaemic, predisposing to nephrocalcinosis and stones.

Many individuals are asymptomatic and detected only through family screening or incidental biochemistry; symptoms, when present, reflect neuromuscular irritability such as paraesthesiae, carpopedal spasm, tetany and seizures.

Correcting the serum calcium to fully normal levels with calcium and active vitamin D is hazardous because it amplifies the underlying hypercalciuria and can precipitate nephrocalcinosis and renal impairment; treatment should be guided by symptoms, not by chasing a normal figure.
Type 2 disease, caused by activation of the Galpha-11 signalling subunit, tends to run a biochemically milder course and has been associated with short stature in some kindreds.
Long-standing hypocalcaemia may lead to basal ganglia calcification and cataract, so these should be sought in chronically affected patients.
Calcium-sensing receptor antagonists (calcilytics) represent an emerging targeted therapeutic approach for this condition.
reference.pathophysiology: Autosomal dominant hypocalcaemia is most often caused by activating (gain-of-function) mutations of the calcium-sensing receptor gene (CASR), giving rise to type 1 disease; a less common type 2 results from activating mutations in GNA11, which encodes the Galpha-11 subunit coupling the receptor to its downstream signalling cascade. The overactive receptor misreads the prevailing extracellular calcium as higher than it truly is, so the parathyroid glands suppress parathyroid hormone secretion at inappropriately low calcium concentrations. In the kidney, receptor activation within the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle diminishes tubular calcium reabsorption and promotes calciuria. The combined result is hypocalcaemia with inappropriately low or normal parathyroid hormone together with relative hypercalciuria. Because the same receptor modulates renal magnesium handling, hypomagnesaemia may coexist, and the reduced calcium reabsorption underlies the tendency to nephrocalcinosis that is aggravated by over-treatment.
additionalDifferentials: Hypoparathyroidism (autoimmune, post-surgical, or associated with 22q11 deletion / DiGeorge)
Pseudohypoparathyroidism, in which parathyroid hormone is elevated because of end-organ resistance
Vitamin D deficiency or hereditary vitamin D-resistant states
additionalInvestigations: Albumin-corrected serum calcium together with ionised calcium
Intact parathyroid hormone measured concurrently with the calcium sample
Timed urinary calcium excretion and the calcium-to-creatinine ratio to demonstrate relative hypercalciuria
Sequencing of CASR and, if negative, GNA11
Renal ultrasound to detect nephrocalcinosis or calculi
Electrocardiogram to assess the corrected QT interval
redFlags: Seizures or laryngospasm from acute severe hypocalcaemia
Prolonged QT interval with attendant risk of arrhythmia
Progressive renal impairment or nephrocalcinosis, often precipitated by over-treatment
reference.prognosis: The outlook is generally good when management is conservative and symptom-guided. The principal long-term threat is renal damage from hypercalciuria, which is worsened rather than prevented by aggressive calcium and active vitamin D replacement.
pitfalls: Mislabelling the condition as idiopathic hypoparathyroidism and treating to a fully normal calcium, thereby precipitating nephrocalcinosis and renal decline.
Failing to measure parathyroid hormone at the same time as calcium, so the inappropriately low value is missed.
Overlooking the family history and not offering screening to at-risk relatives.
Neglecting coexistent hypomagnesaemia, which can perpetuate the hypocalcaemia.
Confusing the direction of the receptor defect with that of familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia.
references: Consensus guidance on hypoparathyroidism and disorders of calcium homeostasis
